**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I sit here, staring at the blank page, the cursor blinking like a metronome counting down the seconds of my indecision. A thousand words—what a strange constraint, what a vast expanse. A thousand words could be a manifesto, a confession, a eulogy, a rant. It could be the beginning of a novel or the end of an argument. It could be nothing at all.

I think about the things I *could* write. I could describe the way the light slants through my window in the late afternoon, turning the dust in the air into golden confetti. I could recount the dream I had last night where I was swimming in a library, the books floating around me like fish, their pages fluttering like gills. I could rant about the absurdity of modern life—how we’re all connected yet so alone, how we scroll endlessly through other people’s curated happiness while our own lives feel like drafts we keep revising but never publish.

But maybe I should write about silence instead. The kind that presses against your eardrums when you’re the last one awake in the house. The kind that hums in the spaces between words when two people who love each other have run out of things to say. Silence isn’t empty; it’s full of all the things we’re too afraid to voice.

Or perhaps I should write about time. How it stretches and contracts like a living thing. How a single minute can feel like an eternity when you’re waiting for test results, or how a decade can vanish in the blink of an eye when you’re lost in a good book. Time is a thief, but it’s also a sculptor—carving us into who we are, one moment at a time.

I remember being a child and believing that adulthood would feel like arrival, like stepping into a room where everything made sense. But adulthood is more like standing in a hallway with a thousand doors, each leading to a different version of your life, and you’re never quite sure which one you’re supposed to open.

What if I wrote about fear? Not the kind that makes your heart race when you watch a horror movie, but the quiet, gnawing fear that keeps you up at night. The fear of irrelevance. The fear of loving someone more than they love you. The fear that you’ll look back on your life and realize you spent it waiting for the *right* moment to begin.

Or maybe I should write about joy. The way it sneaks up on you—like the first sip of coffee on a cold morning, or the sound of laughter spilling from a room before you even know what’s funny. Joy isn’t always loud; sometimes it’s the quiet hum of contentment when you realize, just for a second, that you’re exactly where you’re supposed to be.

I could write about the internet, this vast digital ocean we’re all drowning in. How it’s given us the world but taken our attention spans. How we know more about strangers on the other side of the planet than we do about our own neighbors. How we’ve replaced depth with breadth, trading real connection for the illusion of it.

But maybe I should write about love. Not the grand, cinematic kind, but the mundane, everyday love. The way your partner makes your coffee just the way you like it without being asked. The way your dog follows you from room to room because your presence is his favorite place to be. The way a friend remembers a small detail you mentioned months ago and brings it up when you least expect it. Love isn’t always fireworks; sometimes it’s the slow, steady burn of a candle that refuses to go out.

I think about the words I’ve already written—how they spill out like water from a cracked cup, messy and unfiltered. A thousand words is both too much and not enough. It’s a drop in the ocean of all the things that could be said, all the stories that could be told.

Maybe the point isn’t to say everything. Maybe the point is to say *something*—to reach out across the void and let someone know they’re not alone in their thoughts, their fears, their small, quiet joys.

So here I am, at the end of these words, wondering if any of them mattered. But maybe that’s not the right question. Maybe the right question is: *Did they feel true?*

And the answer, I think, is yes.
